title: Ezekiel 23:11–21
context: The LORD continues speaking to the prophet, saying that Oholibah (Jerusalem) saw what happened to her sister yet went further, turning first to Assyria and then to the Chaldeans, whom she saw portrayed on walls and to whom she sent messengers, before turning from them and back toward Egypt. The chapter’s strong imagery of unfaithfulness is described here only in general terms; it portrays Judah’s shifting alliances (cf. 2 Kgs 16:7; 20:12–13; Ezek 17:15) as betrayal of the covenant. Both traditions read this as shared ground: Jerusalem’s guilt is greater because she saw her sister’s judgment and did not turn (cf. Jer 3:6–11).

verses.text: “Her sister Oholibah saw this, yet she was more corrupt in her lusting than she, and in her prostitution which was more depraved than the prostitution of her sister.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Her sister Oholibah saw this, yet she was more corrupt.” Arminian readers note that Jerusalem’s guilt is heightened because she had seen Samaria’s fall.

Jeremiah 3:6–11 makes a similar comparison between the two sisters.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see greater accountability where there is greater warning.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that witnessing judgment should lead to repentance, and both name Jeremiah 3 without harmonizing it with this chapter.

verses.text: She lusted after the Assyrians, governors and rulers—her neighbors, clothed most gorgeously, horsemen riding on horses, all of them desirable young men.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says Oholibah also turned to the Assyrians, “governors and rulers—her neighbors.” Arminian readers note that Judah repeated Samaria’s path (cf. 2 Kgs 16:7).

The same description of Assyrian splendor returns.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the same temptation drawing Judah away from trust in the LORD.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that Jerusalem relied on Assyria as Samaria had, despite what that reliance had brought on her sister.

verses.text: I saw that she was defiled. They both went the same way.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I saw that she was defiled. They both went the same way.” Arminian readers note the LORD’s verdict that both sisters followed one path.

The verse is brief and direct.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the two kingdoms sharing one pattern of unfaithfulness.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the LORD’s plain assessment that Judah and Israel both broke covenant, which prepares for the shared cup of 23:31–33.

verses.text: “She increased her prostitution; for she saw men portrayed on the wall, the images of the Chaldeans portrayed with red,
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says Oholibah “saw men portrayed on the wall, the images of the Chaldeans portrayed with red.” Arminian readers note that Judah was drawn to Babylon by images of its power.

The detail suggests attraction through display and reputation.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the heart drawn by what the eyes admire.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Judah turning toward the Chaldeans, and both avoid speculation about what specific images may be meant.

verses.text: dressed with belts on their waists, with flowing turbans on their heads, all of them looking like princes, after the likeness of the Babylonians in Chaldea, the land of their birth.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Chaldeans are described “with flowing turbans on their heads, all of them looking like princes.” Arminian readers note the allure of Babylonian royalty and dress.

The description emphasizes outward glory.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the appeal of worldly majesty.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the verse portrays the lure of a rising empire, which drew Judah away from trust in the LORD.

verses.text: As soon as she saw them, she lusted after them and sent messengers to them into Chaldea.
verses.arminianNotes:
Oholibah “sent messengers to them into Chaldea.” Arminian readers note that Judah took the initiative in seeking Babylon’s favor.

Some connect this with the envoys of Hezekiah’s day (cf. 2 Kgs 20:12–13), though the link is not stated.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see Judah actively pursuing foreign alliance.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as political reliance portrayed as unfaithfulness, and both hold any specific historical identification lightly.

verses.text: The Babylonians came to her into the bed of love, and they defiled her with their prostitution. She was polluted with them, and her soul was alienated from them.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD describes the Babylonians defiling Oholibah in strong imagery, and then says that “her soul was alienated from them.” Arminian readers note that the alliance soured.

The imagery is described here only in general terms.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the emptiness of trusting in human powers.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Judah turning from Babylon after relying on it, a pattern of shifting loyalties rather than return to the LORD.

verses.text: So she uncovered her prostitution and uncovered her nakedness. Then my soul was alienated from her, just like my soul was alienated from her sister.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “Then my soul was alienated from her, just like my soul was alienated from her sister.” Arminian readers note the grief and distance in the LORD’s words.

The relationship has been broken by Jerusalem’s unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God’s holy response to persistent sin.

Shared ground: both traditions describe the first half of the verse only in general terms, and both read the LORD’s alienation as the covenant consequence of Jerusalem’s choices.

verses.text: Yet she multiplied her prostitution, remembering the days of her youth, in which she had played the prostitute in the land of Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says Oholibah kept returning to her unfaithfulness, “remembering the days of her youth” in Egypt. Arminian readers note that Judah turned back toward Egypt (cf. 17:15).

The past is remembered wrongly, with longing rather than repentance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the pull of old sins on the heart.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Judah’s renewed reliance on Egypt, and both note that the exodus, which should have been remembered with gratitude, is instead recalled as a source of temptation.

verses.text: She lusted after their lovers, whose flesh is as the flesh of donkeys, and whose issue is like the issue of horses.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD uses deliberately coarse imagery to describe Oholibah’s pursuit of Egypt. Arminian readers note that the language is meant to shock the hearers into seeing their alliances as the LORD sees them.

It is not repeated here.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read the imagery as an intentional rebuke of Judah’s political trust in Egypt.

Shared ground: both traditions describe the verse only in general terms and read it as prophetic shock language aimed at covenant unfaithfulness.

verses.text: Thus you called to memory the lewdness of your youth, in the caressing of your nipples by the Egyptians because of your youthful breasts.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD addresses Oholibah directly, saying she called to memory the unfaithfulness of her youth in Egypt. Arminian readers note the shift to direct address.

The imagery is described here only in general terms.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the LORD confronting Jerusalem with her long history of turning away.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly as the close of the indictment, before the LORD announces judgment in 23:22.
